say.text: Eleven new cases, mixed across the survey. Some stems offer a hint and some are cold. A wrong pick gets a retry or a Show me why.
Last point: the secondary survey and AMPLE history start only after the primary survey and resuscitation. Your review cards cover the core ideas, so go through them over the coming days.
That choice is not right.

Instant deaths feel like the classic trauma death, but this man survives the first minutes and bleeds over hours. He lived past minutes, so he is not in the first peak; that one is reduced only by prevention.
That choice is not right.
Sepsis is the textbook late killer, so the third peak feels familiar. But it comes days to weeks after injury. His deterioration is over 90 minutes, so the timing is hours, not days.
Time it. Count from the injury to the death, and ask which peak is measured in minutes to hours.
A 35-year-old drives into a wall, is awake at the scene, then his pressure drifts down over 90 minutes from a ruptured spleen. Which death peak is he in?

choices.label: First peak: seconds to minutes, from brain or great-vessel injury
Second peak: minutes to several hours, from major blood loss
Third peak: days to weeks, from sepsis and organ failure
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Right. A bleeding spleen over hours is the second peak, the peak ATLS targets.
The answer is the second peak: minutes to several hours after injury, from major blood loss. The first peak is seconds to minutes; the third is days to weeks.
That choice is not right.

More pressure seems the answer to rising pressures, but positive pressure feeds a one-way leak and raises the trapped pressure further. Decompress the chest first; positive pressure adds air to a space that cannot empty.
That choice is not right.
A film feels careful before a procedure, but tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis and this patient is in shock. Do not wait for a film; the bedside findings are enough.
That choice is not right.

That is the classic key site, so it feels familiar. In adults ATLS 10th edition uses the 4th or 5th space. For an adult, the 10th edition site is the 4th or 5th space, anterior to the mid-axillary line.
A 40-year-old, intubated in the bay after a crash, drops to BP 70 with rising airway pressures. The right chest is hyper-resonant with no breath sounds, and the neck veins are full. What next?

choices.label: Give larger breaths to overcome the resistance
Send for a portable chest film to confirm the side
Needle at the 2nd space in the mid-clavicular line
Needle decompression, 4th or 5th space, anterior to mid-axillary line

say.text: Right. The diagnosis is clinical, so you decompress now at the adult site.
The answer: needle decompression now at the 4th or 5th space, anterior to the mid-axillary line. Positive pressure and a film both delay relief of the trapped air.
That choice is not right.
Low pressure in trauma usually means blood loss, so bleeding comes to mind first. Haemorrhage speeds the pulse up. A slow pulse with warm skin points elsewhere.
That choice is not right.
Warm skin and low pressure are the septic picture, so it is tempting. But minutes after a fall, sepsis is not the mechanism. Sepsis is a late problem. Here a cord injury removes sympathetic tone.
Look at the pulse and the skin together. Ask which mechanism slows the heart and keeps the skin warm.
After a fall, a man with a T6 spinal injury has systolic BP 80, pulse 50 and warm dry skin. What type of shock is this?

choices.label: Haemorrhagic shock, since low pressure in trauma means bleeding
Septic shock, since the skin is warm and the pressure is low
Neurogenic shock, from loss of sympathetic tone
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Right. Spinal injury drops the pressure and slows the pulse, with warm skin.
The answer is neurogenic shock: the cord injury removes sympathetic tone, so pressure falls with a slow pulse. Haemorrhagic shock speeds the pulse.
That choice is not right.
One surgical airway for all seems simpler to remember, but the cricoid is at risk in a child. Under about 12 years the surgical route is avoided; age changes the choice.
That choice is not right.

A needle sounds safer for everyone, so one rule feels neat. But the adult route of choice is surgical. The adult emergency surgical airway is surgical cricothyroidotomy; the needle route is for the child.
One rule changes at about 12 years. Ask which patient it protects, and why.
Intubation fails and oxygen cannot be delivered in two patients: a 9-year-old and a 30-year-old. Which emergency surgical airway for each?

choices.label: Surgical cricothyroidotomy for the adult, needle for the child
Needle cricothyroidotomy for both, as the safer route
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Right. Adults get the surgical route; under about 12 years a needle route is used.
The answer: surgical cricothyroidotomy for the 30-year-old, needle cricothyroidotomy for the 9-year-old. The cutoff is about 12 years, because the cricoid is at risk in children.
That choice is not right.
The bleeding is the loudest problem, so it feels first. But the order follows speed of death, and haemorrhage control sits inside C. Airway and breathing come before circulation in the ATLS order.
That choice is not right.

He is speaking, so it feels like he is stable. But talking shows an open airway only for the moment, and his breathing is poor. Short phrases and fast shallow breaths mean breathing needs attention now.
A cyclist hit by a van talks in short phrases. His thigh is bleeding steadily and his breathing is fast and shallow. What do you do first?

choices.label: Put a tourniquet on the thigh, since bleeding kills most
Move on to the secondary survey, since he is talking
Reassess airway and breathing now, and treat problems before the bleed

say.text: Right. Talking in short phrases with fast shallow breathing needs B dealt with first; the bleed is handled in C.
The answer: reassess airway and breathing first, then control the bleed under C. The order follows what kills fastest, and talking only shows the airway for the moment.
That choice is not right.

Two litres is the figure older keys print, so it feels standard. ATLS 10th edition gives 1 L warmed, with early blood. The current adult bolus is 1 L warmed isotonic crystalloid; large volumes dilute clotting and cool the patient.
That choice is not right.
Eight hours sticks in memory as the limit, so waiting feels safe. But 8 hours is the infusion; the start window is 3 hours. He is at 2 hours, inside the window. Waiting risks missing it.
An adult weighing 70 kg arrives 2 hours after a crash with a bleeding pelvis and BP 80/50. Which initial plan is right?

choices.label: 2 L crystalloid fast, then blood if there is no response
1 L warmed crystalloid, early blood, TXA now
Hold TXA until CT, as it works up to 8 hours

say.text: Right. This is the 10th edition bolus, early blood, and TXA still inside its 3-hour window.
The answer: 1 L warmed crystalloid, early blood, and TXA now. Exam note: older keys print 2 L. TXA starts within 3 hours of injury; the 8 hours is the second infusion.
That choice is not right.
He cannot pass urine, so a catheter feels like the obvious relief. But these signs suggest a urethral tear. A catheter is held back until a urethrogram shows an intact urethra.
That choice is not right.
CT is the thorough test, so it feels careful. But an unstable patient should not go to the scanner. Use the bedside test in the room; imaging waits for stability.
A cyclist falls astride the bar. He has perineal bruising and a high-riding prostate, cannot pass urine, and has an unstable pelvis with BP 85. What comes before any catheter?

choices.label: A Foley catheter now, to relieve the retention and measure urine
CT of the abdomen and pelvis, to map the injury
A retrograde urethrogram to check the urethra

say.text: Right. The urethra is checked first, and the catheter goes in only if it is intact.
The answer: a retrograde urethrogram first. Perineal bruising and a high-riding prostate suggest a torn urethra, and the catheter must wait.
That choice is not right.

The moving segment is the visible problem, so fixing it feels like treating the cause. But it is the sign, not the cause. The hypoxia comes from the lung beneath the segment, so treatment goes to the lung.
That choice is not right.
Rib fractures often bring a pneumothorax, so it feels likely. But the main cause here is the contusion beneath the segment. The contusion drives the low oxygen, not a simple pneumothorax.
An older man falls and breaks three ribs on the right, each in two places. A segment moves paradoxically and his saturation is 88%. Which statement is right?

choices.label: Fixing the moving segment will correct the hypoxia
A small simple pneumothorax is the main cause of the hypoxia
The bruised lung is the cause; oxygen, analgesia, ventilate if needed

say.text: Right. The pulmonary contusion causes the hypoxia, so treatment targets the lung.
The answer: the underlying pulmonary contusion is the main cause. The paradoxical movement marks the injury, and treatment goes to the lung.
That choice is not right.

Permissive hypotension is a real strategy for bleeding, so it seems right for her. But it is not used with a brain injury. The injured brain needs perfusion; secondary brain injury follows low pressure and low oxygen.
That choice is not right.

Pushing fluid is the reflex for a low pressure, and 2 L is the older figure. But large volumes worsen bleeding, and the 10th edition bolus is 1 L. Use a smaller warmed bolus with early blood while keeping the brain perfused.
A woman with a bleeding spleen also has a head injury, GCS 7, and a systolic BP of 85. The surgeon wants to run the pressure low until theatre. What is right?

choices.label: Agree, because a low pressure protects the clot in any bleeding patient
Give 2 L crystalloid fast to bring the pressure up
Keep pressure high enough to perfuse the brain; find the bleeding

say.text: Right. Permissive hypotension is not used in brain injury, so the brain is kept perfused.
The answer: keep perfusion adequate for the brain and control the bleeding. Permissive hypotension is not used in traumatic brain injury.
That choice is not right.
Normal numbers are reassuring, so shock feels excluded. But beta-blockers and age blunt the heart-rate response. Tachycardia can be absent, so pale cool skin and confusion are signs to act on.
That choice is not right.
Class II seems like it should already lower the pressure. But hypotension first appears in Class III. A normal BP does not exclude shock; compensation holds the pressure.
A 72-year-old on a beta-blocker falls. Pulse 78, BP 118/76, skin cool and pale, and he is confused. How do you read this?

choices.label: No shock, since the pulse and BP are both normal
Early shock only, since hypotension would already show by Class II
Shock may be present, since drugs and age blunt the usual signs

say.text: Right. Pale cool skin and confusion are warnings when tachycardia is blunted.
The answer: shock may be present. Beta-blockers and age can hide tachycardia, and hypotension appears late, in Class III, so act on the skin and mental state.
That choice is not right.

Low pressure with full neck veins looks like a pressure problem in the pleura. But tension pneumothorax gives a silent, hyper-resonant side and a deviated trachea. Here the breath sounds are equal and the trachea is central.
That choice is not right.
A chest wound with shock makes blood loss the first thought. But haemothorax gives a dull, silent side, and both sides are clear here. Look for one-sided dullness; there is none.
That choice is not right.

A collapsed lung looks like it should drag things toward it. But a collapsed lung does not give this picture, and in tension the mediastinum is pushed away. The findings here point to the heart, not a pleural collapse.
A man is shot in the left chest. BP 70, neck veins distended, heart sounds faint, trachea central, and breath sounds clear and equal. What is the likely diagnosis?

choices.label: Tension pneumothorax, since low BP and full neck veins fit
Massive haemothorax, since shock after a chest wound means blood
Cardiac tamponade, with blood around the heart
A collapsed lung, which pulls the mediastinum toward the injured side

say.text: Right. Hypotension, muffled heart sounds and distended neck veins with clear lungs is Beck's triad.
The answer: cardiac tamponade. Beck's triad with clear, equal breath sounds and a central trachea points to the pericardium, not the pleura.

cards.q: What sets the order of the primary survey?
cards.a: Speed of death: airway in minutes, then breathing, then circulation with haemorrhage control.

cards.q: What does a patient who talks normally show?
cards.a: A patent airway, breathing and cerebral perfusion for the moment; the next step is breathing, not intubation.

cards.q: Emergency surgical airway: adult versus a child under 12?
cards.a: Surgical cricothyroidotomy in adults; needle cricothyroidotomy under about 12, since the cricoid can be damaged.

cards.q: When and where is tension pneumothorax decompressed?
cards.a: At once, on clinical diagnosis; in adults at the 4th or 5th intercostal space, anterior to the mid-axillary line.

cards.q: How do tension pneumothorax, massive haemothorax and tamponade differ?
cards.a: Tension: hyper-resonance, trachea away, distended neck veins. Haemothorax: dullness, flat neck veins. Tamponade: muffled heart sounds, Beck's triad.

cards.q: Where does hypotension first appear in haemorrhagic shock?
cards.a: Class III, 31 to 40 percent loss. Neurogenic shock gives hypotension with bradycardia; normal vitals mislead in the elderly and beta-blocked.

cards.q: Initial adult crystalloid, and the brain-injury target?
cards.a: 1 L warmed isotonic crystalloid in ATLS 10th edition, where the older key gave 2 L; permissive hypotension is not used in brain injury.

cards.q: Unstable patient: CT or FAST? And before a catheter in urethral injury?
cards.a: FAST in the resuscitation room; a retrograde urethrogram before any catheter.

cards.q: Which antifibrinolytic, and within what time?
cards.a: Tranexamic acid within 3 hours of injury: 1 g over 10 minutes, then 1 g over 8 hours.
